vignette: David Miller had spent twenty years as a school principal, but the incident in the sublevel storage room twelve months ago had fractured that certainty. It had happened after a late staff training; the main corridor was empty when a disheveled man emerged from the equipment alcove. He pressed the cold steel of a folding knife against David’s ribs, forcing him backward until his spine met the cinderblock wall. The intruder demanded his wallet before vanishing. When responders arrived, David realized that whenever he tried to deliberately remember what happened, he found it difficult to access the memory. The timeline refused to assemble. Yet his mind refused to let it rest. Within weeks, his memories of the frightening event were like a film that played over and over. They returned unbidden, bypassing his conscious control. Whenever memories of what happened came to mind, he felt his body was in the same position as when the frightening event occurred: shoulders hiked, calves locked into the exact braced posture he had held against the wall. The sudden intrusion of that bodily tension acted as a direct switch for his threat system. His nervous system interpreted the physical reenactment as a live emergency, immediately flooding him with a jumpy or easily startled state. He found himself scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room or building, his gaze tracking every possible way out. His attention automatically noticed potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, reading a letter opener or a heavy chair base not as office supplies but as imminent threats. The school rapidly transformed into a landscape of ambushes. He managed the pattern by shrinking his presence. After-school visits to the administrative wing became impossible; the echoing hallways triggered the same reflex, forcing him to leave through the side entrance and avoid the main corridor. He delegated every night meeting to his vice principal, though he knew the truth. At home, the vigilance bled into their marriage. Elena noticed how he flinched when the porch light clicked on, how he positioned his chair with his back to the drywall and his eyes fixed on the front door. He told himself he was simply being careful, that he had learned how quickly safety could vanish, but the constant scanning drained his stamina. The cycle tightened without warning: an involuntary memory replay would seize his posture, spike his startle response, and lock his vision on potential weapons or escape routes, feeding more fragmented recollections. The breaking point arrived during a budget review. A misplaced stapler had clattered to the floor, and David’s entire body seized, his breath catching as the memory replayed with full visceral force. He had to excuse himself, pacing the corridor until his heart rate finally descended. That evening, sitting across from Elena, he finally admitted he could no longer navigate his own building without feeling his chest tighten and his eyes darting to the corners. He came to therapy hoping to quiet the relentless replay, to stop his body from treating every shadow like the man in the storage room. He feared losing his career, but what he wanted most was to walk through his school again and simply feel the ground beneath his feet.
